summary_md: Porter, Case and Treul (Scientific Data 2025) release CampaignView, a data descriptor rather than a hypothesis test: campaign-website text for U.S. House major-party primary candidates in 2018, 2020 and 2022. Of 6,016 ballot-eligible candidates, 5,228 (86.9%) are in the corpus, giving 43,465 platform points and 5,114 biographies. Text was scraped about one week before each primary, with Wayback Machine backfill (7.8% of candidates). Every platform point is hand-coded into one of 14 policy topics. On a 20% relabel sample (8,584 points) agreement is 80% and Cohen kappa is 0.84. Rows carry FEC and BioGuide IDs, and candidate names were linked across cycles by embedding-based record linkage. Missingness is not random: across the 6,016 candidates, 11.9% have no website and 25.1% have no platform, and incumbents, unopposed candidates and better-funded candidates are much less likely to be missing (Table 5 logit, associations only). In descriptive platform shares, Democrats emphasize environment, healthcare and social welfare, while Republicans emphasize immigration and government operations. For Paul's systems the paper has no network, lobbying or allocation content. It matters in two places. First, the electoral-plays contest-primary route scores an Opponent's primary vulnerability against the same-party average CU score, not against any real challenger. CampaignView gives candidate-level challenger platforms that could replace that proxy for House seats in 2018-2022. Second, its hand-coded topic labels with reported reliability are a template for the open question of how precise the press-release regex topic tagger is. Coverage limits: House only, three cycles, website text only. The topic codes do not map to credit-union categories.

bearings.paper_claim: Platform text exists for 5,228 of 6,016 (86.9%) House major-party primary candidates 2018-2022, including challengers, keyed by FEC ID and BioGuideID; 43,465 hand-topic-coded platform points.
bearings.paper_location: Abstract p.1; Methods p.4; Data Records p.5
bearings.system_side: The contest route scores primary vulnerability as the sum of an Opponent member's negative CU-score gaps against the same-party AVERAGE (avgP), a proxy for a generic primary challenger; no actual challenger data enters.
bearings.transfer_conditions: House seats only, cycles 2018-2022 (stale for 119th Congress challengers); topics are 14 general policy codes, not CU categories, so a challenger CU stance would need a new reader. Challenger missingness is highest for low-fundraising, uncompetitive candidates, exactly the ones the gap matters least for. New analysis UNVERIFIED until reproduced (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: Each platform point hand-coded by trained annotators to one of 14 Major Policy Topic codes with a codebook; 20% relabel (8,584 points) gave 80% agreement, Cohen kappa 0.84, weighted kappa 0.74, with disagreement concentrated in Unknown/Other.
bearings.paper_location: Methods p.3; Technical Validation p.10; Table 6 crosswalk
bearings.system_side: Press-release categories are assigned by regex term lists (19 Layer-2 categories); the component's open question is regex precision against human coding, which has no recorded human benchmark.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Transfers as a validation design (double-code a random sample, report kappa), not as labels: genre differs (campaign platforms vs official press releases) and the topic scheme differs from CU categories. The single-topic-per-item rule under-codes multi-topic text, a caveat that also applies to the regex tagger.

bearings.paper_claim: Cross-cycle candidate names linked by probabilistic record linkage on pretrained word embeddings, blocked on party and state, matches under 50% hand-checked; 15 wrong matches 2018-2020, 1 for 2020-2022, 0 for 2018-2022.
bearings.system_side: Contributor identity uses an ordered rule ladder (name parts, zip, city, occupation, employer contradiction) with no name-frequency weighting; member names resolve through member_identity Resolver, which accepts bioguide.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Paper links candidates (small, ID-rich population), not individual donors; error counts are for candidate names only and do not speak to donor-level false-match rates.

gaps_exposed: electoral-plays primary route uses the same-party average as a stand-in challenger; no actual primary-challenger data (positions, fundraising, quality) enters the contest value.
No human-coded reliability benchmark (kappa or precision) exists for the regex press-release topic tagger; CampaignView shows the minimal design (20% double-code).
Systems have no campaign-stage issue-emphasis input; whether a member's campaign platform emphasis predicts later CU-relevant press or legislative priority is untested.
flags: No conflict with brain rules: paper makes no network, closeness, influence or LDA claims.
Table 5 missingness coefficients are pooled across parties and cycles; quote as UNSTRATIFIED associations if cited.
Item kind corrected upstream to data descriptor; abstract says 5,228 corpus candidates while Methods says 5,300 had a website; both figures use denominator 6,016.
paul_alignment: No annotated-bibliography entry and no markup from Paul for this work, so there is no takeaway to check. Nothing is stale.

related.why: Bonica places candidates by donor money (CFscores); CampaignView supplies their stated platform text. Together they allow say-versus-funded position checks for the same FEC-ID-keyed candidates.
Broockman studies the electoral payoff of candidate positioning; CampaignView is a candidate-level source of the positions taken in primaries.
CampaignView hand-codes 43,465 points; Ornstein shows LLM coding of political text, the scalable alternative whose output could be checked against CampaignView's kappa-validated labels.
